<div>
### Stock Performance Analyzer
<p class="project-type">Financial analytics · Python · CSV · Plotly · pytest</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The user supplies a Nasdaq historical-price CSV. The program parses price and volume records, calculates closing-price statistics, total and daily returns, and volatility, then prints a summary and includes an interactive HTML-report generator. It is meaningful because it connects file processing, tested financial calculations, and visual communication in one course project.

#### How it works

CSV rows are converted into a date-keyed dictionary. Separate functions sort dates and calculate each measure; six pytest functions define expected results for the core numeric logic, while Plotly figures support the report layer.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from stock_analyzer.py</summary>

```python
def calculate_total_return(stock_dict):
    date_list = []
    for date in stock_dict:
        converted_date = dt.datetime.strptime(date,"%m/%d/%Y")
        date_list.append((converted_date, date))
    start_date = min(date_list)
    end_date = max(date_list)
    start_price = stock_dict[start_date[1]]["close"]
    end_price = stock_dict[end_date[1]]["close"]
    total_return = ((end_price - start_price) / start_price) * 100
    return total_return
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> Dates are converted before comparison, so total return uses the true beginning and end of the period instead of relying on CSV row order.</p>

<span class="course-rank">02</span>
<div>
### Retail Receipt and Product Lookup
<p class="project-type">Python · CSV processing · Dictionaries · Error handling · pytest</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The program combines a product catalog with a separate customer request file to produce an itemized retail receipt. It reports quantities, subtotal, sales tax, total, current time, and a return deadline while handling missing files, permission errors, and unknown product IDs.

#### How it works

A reusable function loads `products.csv` into a dictionary keyed by product number. The main routine loops through `request.csv`, uses each ID for a dictionary lookup, accumulates quantities and prices, and formats the final receipt; a pytest file validates the catalog-loading function.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from receipt.py</summary>

```python
def read_dictionary(filename,key_column_index):
    products_dict = {}
    with open(filename, "rt") as csv_file:
        reader = csv.reader(csv_file)
        next(reader)
        for row in reader:
            if len(row) != 0:
                key = row[key_column_index]
                products_dict[key] = row
    return products_dict
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> A configurable key column turns CSV rows into a reusable lookup dictionary that supports the receipt workflow.</p>
:::

::: {.course-detail}
::: {.course-heading}
<span class="course-rank">03</span>
<div>
### Water Distribution Calculations
<p class="project-type">Python · Functions · Engineering calculations · pytest</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The user supplies water-tower, tank, pipe-length, and fitting inputs. The program estimates pressure at a house after calculating the starting water pressure and subtracting losses from pipes, fittings, and a pipe-size reduction. It is a substantial example of translating a multi-stage quantitative model into reusable functions.

#### How it works

Six focused functions implement the individual formulas, including Reynolds number and pressure loss. `main()` applies constants for the two pipe types and executes the calculations in sequence; a companion pytest module provides approximate numeric expectations for each function.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from w3_water_flow.py</summary>

```python
def water_column_height(tower_height, tank_height):
    height = tower_height + (3 * tank_height)/4
    return height

def pressure_gain_from_water_height(height):
    pressure = WATER_DENSITY * EARTH_ACCELERATION_OF_GRAVITY * height /1000
    return pressure

def pressure_loss_from_pipe(pipe_diameter, pipe_length, friction_factor, fluid_velocity):
    lost_pressure = -friction_factor * pipe_length * WATER_DENSITY * (fluid_velocity**2) / (2000 * pipe_diameter)
    return lost_pressure
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> A multi-stage engineering model is separated into small calculation functions that can be checked independently.</p>
:::

::: {.course-detail}
::: {.course-heading}
<span class="course-rank">04</span>
<div>
### Student ID CSV Lookup
<p class="project-type">Python · CSV processing · Dictionaries · Testing</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The user enters a student I-number and receives the corresponding name when that identifier exists in the supplied CSV. The assignment demonstrates how a lookup-oriented data structure can replace repeated searching and how file-loading behavior can be tested independently.

#### How it works

`read_dictionary()` skips the CSV header and stores every non-empty record under a configurable key column. `main()` checks the entered I-number against that dictionary, while the companion tests verify file handling, the returned type, and expected records.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from W5_students.py</summary>

```python
def read_dictionary(filename, key_column_index):
    students_dict = {}
    with open(filename, "rt") as csv_file:
            reader = csv.reader(csv_file)
            next(reader)
            for row in reader:
               if len(row) !=0:
                   key = row[key_column_index]
                   students_dict[key] = row
    return students_dict
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> Structured CSV records are indexed by a meaningful identifier for direct user-driven lookup.</p>
:::

::: {.course-detail}

<div>
### Life Expectancy Data Analysis
<p class="project-type">Python · Data analysis · CSV processing · Aggregation</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The user chooses a question about a global life-expectancy CSV containing more than 19,000 country-year records. The program reports overall extremes, summarizes a selected year or country, or identifies the largest consecutive recorded decline within a country. It is the course’s strongest example of turning a large structured file into focused analytical answers.

#### How it works

Each menu branch reads the file, skips its header, splits records into country, code, year, and numeric life-expectancy fields, then filters or aggregates them. Lists support average calculations, while running comparisons track maximums, minimums, and adjacent declines.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from Data_Analysis.py</summary>

```python
with open("life-expectancy.csv") as life_data:
    next(life_data)
    for line in life_data:
        data_stripped = line.strip().split(",")
        country = data_stripped[0]
        code = data_stripped[1]
        year = data_stripped[2]
        age = float(data_stripped[3])
        if year == user_year:
            count += 1
            ages.append(age)
            if age > user_highest_value:
                user_highest_value = age
                user_highest_country = country
                user_highest_year = year
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> One pass through a structured file combines parsing, filtering, numeric conversion, collection building, and running extrema.</p>

<div>
### Shopping Cart
<p class="project-type">Python · Lists · Loops · Menu-driven design</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The user manages a command-line shopping cart by adding named items and prices, reviewing numbered contents, removing an item, and requesting the total. The project is meaningful because several state-changing operations share the same in-memory data across a repeated menu.

#### How it works

Parallel lists keep item names aligned with prices. An outer loop keeps the menu active until quit, nested loops accept multiple additions and display contents, and list indexes connect a user-facing item number to removal and total calculations.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from shopping_cart.py</summary>

```python
while customer_input != 5:

    print()
    if customer_input == 1:
        print("What items would you like to add? (type 'done' when finished adding items)")
        new_item = input("")
        print()
        while new_item != 'done':
            new_price = float(input("How much does this item cost? "))
            print()
            price_list.append(new_price)
            item_list.append(new_item.capitalize())
            new_item = input("Another item? ")
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> Nested loops maintain cart state across repeated menu actions while keeping item names aligned with their prices.</p>

<span class="course-rank">03</span>
<div>
### Windchill Calculator
<p class="project-type">Python · Functions · Unit conversion · Iterative calculations</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The user provides a temperature and identifies whether it is Fahrenheit or Celsius. The program converts the value when necessary and reports windchill at five-mile-per-hour increments through 60 mph. It turns a scientific formula into a repeatable comparative output rather than a single calculation.

#### How it works

One function normalizes the temperature to Fahrenheit and another encapsulates the windchill equation. A loop increases wind speed by five on each pass and sends the shared temperature and current speed into the calculation function.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from Windchill.py</summary>

```python
def conversion(user_choice,temp):
    if user_choice == "C":
        F = temp * (9/5) +32
        return F
    else:
        return temp

def windchill(new_temp,wind):
    windchill = 35.74 + 0.6215*(new_temp) - 35.75*(wind**0.16) + 0.4275*(new_temp)*(wind**0.16)
    return windchill
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> Unit conversion and the windchill formula are isolated as reusable functions rather than embedded in the output loop.</p>
:::

::: {.course-detail}
::: {.course-heading}
<span class="course-rank">04</span>
<div>
### Word Puzzle
<p class="project-type">Python · String analysis · Loops · Conditional logic</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The player has a limited number of attempts to identify a secret word. After each valid-length guess, the program distinguishes letters in the correct position, letters found elsewhere in the word, and absent letters. This creates a compact but meaningful string-comparison algorithm with repeated feedback.

#### How it works

The main loop stops when the answer is correct or the attempt limit is reached. An inner index loop compares every guessed character against the same position in the secret and then against the complete secret, changing case or printing a placeholder to encode the result.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from word_puzzle.py</summary>

```python
while guess != secret and guesses < max_guesses:
    print()

    guess = input("What is your guess? ").lower()

    guesses += 1

    print(f"You have {max_guesses - guesses} guesses left. ")

    if len(guess) != len(secret):
        print("Sorry, the guess must have the same number of letters as the secret word.")
    else:
          for i in range(len(guess)):
            if guess[i] == secret[i]:
                 print(guess[i].upper(), end=" ")
            elif guess[i] in secret:
                 print(guess[i].lower(), end=" ")
            else:
                print("_", end=" ")
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> Indexed character comparisons encode three different feedback states inside a bounded guessing loop.</p>
:::

::: {.course-detail}
::: {.course-heading}
<span class="course-rank">05</span>
<div>
### Branching Adventure Game
<p class="project-type">Python · Branching logic · Input normalization · Program flow</p>
</div>
:::

#### Purpose

The player enters a character name and makes decisions through a multi-stage narrative. Each choice leads to another scenario or one of several success and failure endings. Its value lies in coordinating a comparatively large branching structure while keeping later choices dependent on earlier decisions.

#### How it works

User responses are normalized with `.lower()` and evaluated through nested `if`, `elif`, and `else` blocks. Each accepted branch prints new context and requests the next decision; fallback branches handle inputs outside the expected choices.

<details class="course-code">
<summary>View real source excerpt from Adventure_game.py</summary>

```python
Q1 = input("Do you get UP or go SLEEP? ")
Q1 = Q1.lower()
if Q1 == "up":
    print()
    print("Sgr Buck: 'Hey bud I know you hit your head real hard but that ain't an excuse to "
        "be napping on duty! Are you gonna just sit there while we win this or are you gonna join us?'")
    print()
    print("*He hands you a rifle*")
    print()
    Q2 = input("Do you TAKE it or RUN? ")
    Q2 = Q2.lower()
    if Q2 == "take":
        print()
        print(f"Sgr Buck: 'Atta boy Private {name.capitalize()}, now lets organize ourselves.'")
        print("Should we charge em, sit back and snipe em or fall back and regroup?'")
        print()
        Q3 = input("Do you CHARGE, SNIPE, or FALL BACK? ")
        Q3 = Q3.lower()
```

</details>

<p class="code-takeaway"><strong>What this demonstrates:</strong> Normalized input and nested conditional branches preserve decision context across multiple stages of an interactive program.</p>
:::
